parsed.summary: This paper presents a note-grounded framework for normalizing treatment-context medication evidence from clinic notes and comparing it with structured electronic health record (EHR) medication history. The study uses a large language model (LLM)-assisted reference construction, human review, and deterministic medication normalization to improve canonical agreement. Results show that normalization errors, differences in terminology, and documentation timing contribute to note-to-structured-medication mismatches, with significant semantic and temporal overlap between the two sources.

chk_problem.value: Discrepancies between clinic notes and structured EHR medication history due to normalization errors, terminology differences, and documentation timing.
chk_problem.paper_quote: Same-visit disagreement between these sources may result from note-side normalization errors, differences in terminology or timing, or actual differences in documentation.

chk_method.value: Note-grounded approach using LLM-assisted reference construction, human review, deterministic normalization, and semantic-temporal comparisons.
chk_method.paper_quote: We developed a note-grounded approach that uses large language model (LLM)-assisted reference construction, targeted and random human review, deterministic medication normalization, and semantic and temporal comparisons with structured medication history.

chk_data.value: 11,812 eligible visits, 761 patients, 22,483 manifest notes, and 27,752 reference mention rows.
chk_data.paper_quote: We conducted a clinic-note-only evaluation of treatment-context medication normalization using a frozen cohort run of 11,812 eligible visits from 761 patients and 22,483 manifest notes.

chk_setup.value: Evaluation on a patient-level held-out test set with 5,403 mention rows and a fixed random seed for patient split.
chk_setup.paper_quote: To reduce within-cohort adaptation risk for technical performance claims, we introduced a patient-level held-out evaluation track.

chk_primary_result.value: Exact canonical agreement improved from 0.7226 to 0.8429 after lexical cleanup and curated alias mapping.
chk_primary_result.paper_quote: On 5,403 held-out mention rows, exact canonical agreement improved from 0.7226 with surface-exact matching to 0.8429 after lexical cleanup and curated alias mapping.

chk_secondary_result.value: 55.17% of note-derived rows had same-visit semantic overlap, and 90.34% had same-visit or ±30-day overlap with structured medication history.
chk_secondary_result.paper_quote: In the full-cohort characterization analysis, only 16.44% of note-derived rows had same-visit exact overlap with structured medication history, but 55.17% had same-visit semantic overlap, 90.34% had same-visit or ±30-day overlap, and only 3.97% remained in the strict no-structured-overlap bucket under broad project-level mapping.

chk_baseline.value: Surface-exact matching and generic lexical retrieval methods, including MedXN as an external baseline.
chk_baseline.paper_quote: As one recognizable external baseline, we also ran untuned MedXN [4] on held-out notes and compared note-level recovery of unique note and normalized-medication-label pairs on a predefined treatment-context subset.

chk_conclusion.value: Evidence characterization should precede clinical inference when comparing clinic-note medication evidence with structured medication history.
chk_conclusion.paper_quote: These results suggest that evidence characterization should precede downstream clinical inference when clinic-note medication evidence is compared with structured medication history.

chk_limitation.value: Single-center cohort, project-specific canonical label space, and non-exhaustive manual annotation of reference set.
chk_limitation.paper_quote: The cohort comes from a private single-center clinic-note environment, and both the canonical label space and broad medication categories are project-specific.
